analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 22%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the top corporate tax rate by 13 points never got a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower the highest corporate income tax rate from 35% to 22%, and would apply the same cut to personal service corporations like law and consulting firms. It would also flatten the corporate rate schedule so nearly all corporations pay the same rate. The bill was introduced in March 2010, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never moved from there.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders would gain the most, since the federal tax bill on corporate profits would drop by up to 13 percentage points. Corporate executives and business lobby groups backing a lower US rate would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum corporate income tax rate from 35% to 22%, including for personal service corporations.
Flattens the corporate rate schedule, striking the brackets that applied different rates to corporate income above $75,000, so the new 22% rate covers all corporate income above the lowest brackets.
Applies to corporate taxable years beginning after December 31, 2009, so the cut would have been retroactive to the current tax year.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury would collect less revenue, meaning the gap would have to be covered by borrowing, other taxes, or lower government spending. The benefits of a corporate rate cut flow mainly to shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income households.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top rate by 13 percentage points would sharply reduce federal revenue on corporate profits, which must be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or reduced spending.

The bill lowers rates without closing any loopholes or preferences, so it reduces revenue without broadening the tax base — an approach even many tax-policy supporters of lower corporate rates say should be paired.
The savings would flow to corporate shareholders rather than directly to workers or consumers; any pass-through to wages is indirect and uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A 13-point cut in the corporate rate is a large, permanent reduction in revenue, and the direct benefit lands on shareholders rather than on working people. The bill makes no attempt to pay for itself or to close loopholes, so even readers sympathetic to the goal of a lower corporate rate would find it an unbalanced design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Todd Tiahrt introduced the bill on March 4, 2010, with one Republican cosponsor.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
The committee held no hearings, markup, or vote on the bill, and no further action was ever recorded before the Congress ended in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury is better off because the bill died: the 13-point corporate rate cut never took effect, so no revenue was lost. Corporate shareholders are worse off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, since the rate cut never happened

for.name: Rep. Todd Tiahrt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the top corporate rate to 22% and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support came from two House Republicans (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never moved it; no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would cut their tax rate by 13 percentage points on all profits, a direct transfer of revenue away from the federal treasury. The cost would fall on taxpayers generally, while the gain goes to shareholders.

industries.industry: Personal service corporations (law, accounting, and consulting firms)
industries.note: These firms pay the top rate and would see it drop from 35% to 22%, a large cut to their tax bills.
After-tax corporate profits would rise under a lower rate, benefiting shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income households.
